USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the tariff posture already in force and restart a negotiation track with Beijing rather than escalating to the threatened additional $267B or rushing further action. Keep the scheduled Jan 1 rise to 25% as standing pressure, and signal willingness to talk once China returns to the table, while pairing this with relief for the farm belt before the midterms.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to US interests is real but contained, so I score it +0.3. List 3 (~$200B at 10%, rising to 25% Jan 1) took effect Sept 24, pushing combined Section 301 coverage to ~$250B, while China retaliated the same day with 5-10% tariffs on ~$60B of US goods including soybeans and pork (NPR/BI, 9/18). That retaliation is targeted squarely at the farm belt — the NYT (4/19) and Globe & Mail (9/23) report GOP incumbents and farm groups warning of midterm losses, and even the $12B aid package is described as an insufficient 'mute button' (Des Moines Register, 8/3). Meanwhile US fundamentals remain strong (IP 104.1, consumer sentiment 100.1, dollar firm ~113.7, unemployment lowest since 2000), whereas China's economy is visibly slowing (Shanghai Comp -20% YTD, RMB slide to ~6.88/$). That asymmetry argues against an existential threat reading — but the collapse of the Liu He talks and domestic political exposure to escalating farm retaliation keep this a mild threat, not a clean US opportunity. On action, I recommend a near-neutral +0.15 stance: the US has already applied maximum pressure and retains leverage through the scheduled 25% tier, so escalating further to $267B now would raise consumer costs exactly ahead of the midterms and harden a deadlock, with no talks venue active. De-escalating unilaterally would forfeit hard-won leverage. Holding and re-engaging diplomatically while relieving farmers is the posture most consistent with both the threat level and US leverage.
key_factors: ~$250B of Chinese imports now under Section 301 tariffs; 25% tier scheduled Jan 1
